summary:
Every cell must be updated from the **old** board, so naively writing new values would corrupt the
neighbour counts of cells not yet visited. Either read from a copy (O(mn) extra space), or store the new
state in a spare bit of each cell, leaving the old state readable until a final pass shifts it out
(O(1) extra space).

question.md:
Apply one generation of the rules to a grid of 0s (empty) and 1s (alive). Each cell looks at its up to 8
neighbours (including diagonals):

- **Alive** with 2 or 3 living neighbours: stays alive. Fewer than 2 or more than 3: dies.
- **Empty** with exactly 3 living neighbours: becomes alive.

- **All cells change at the same moment**, based on the old board. This is the whole difficulty.
- **Edges and corners** simply have fewer neighbours (5 or 3); nothing wraps around.
- **Size:** up to 200 × 200, so the work is tiny; the interesting constraint is "without a second grid".

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- Border and corner cells have fewer than eight neighbours.
- A 1 × 1 board: the single cell has no neighbours, so a living cell dies.
- All updates are simultaneous: births and deaths must not affect each other's counts.

think.md:
**Simultaneous updates.** Every cell's new value must be computed from the **old** values of its neighbours. Writing
new values straight into the grid breaks that: a neighbour processed later would read an already-updated cell. The
easy fix is a copy of the grid. The in-place fix is to store **both** the old and the new value in the same cell, using
spare bits:

- old value in the low bits (read with a mask, `x & 1` or `x & 255`);
- new value in the higher bits (written with `|=` and a shift);
- one final pass shifts every cell right, keeping only the new value.

**Rules:** alive with 2 or 3 neighbours → stays alive; empty with exactly 3 → born; otherwise empty.

**Two states in one cell.** Bit 0 holds the current state; bit 1 holds the next state. Counting reads `x & 1`, so
it only ever sees the old state, even for cells already processed. After marking:
Shifting every cell right by one keeps the next state:

approaches.title: Count from a copy of the board

idea.md: Copy the board; count each cell's living neighbours in the copy and write the new state into the board.

lines.text: A frozen snapshot of the current generation. All reading happens here.

notes.c: Here the input stays untouched and serves as the snapshot; the next generation is written into a fresh grid.

lines.text: Every cell gets its new state.
Sum the 3 × 3 block around the cell, clipped at the borders (`max(0, …)` / `min(…, last)`), then subtract the cell itself: what's left is its living neighbours.
Alive next if it has exactly 3 neighbours, or 2 and is alive now. Every other case is empty.

notes.c: Report the row count and every row's length; the caller frees the new grid.

complexity.md: **Time O(m · n)** (up to 8 neighbours each). **Space O(m · n)** for the copy.

steps.text: Copy the board. Every count below reads the copy, so updates never disturb later counts.
All cells done the same way.

walk.title: Read neighbours from an untouched copy; write the next generation into the board.

limits.md: A full copy of the board just to remember old values; each cell has spare bits that can hold the new value instead.

approaches.title: Two states in one cell (bit tricks)

idea.md:
Pass 1: for each cell, count neighbours with `& 1` (old state only) and, if the cell will be alive, set bit
1 (`|= 2`). Pass 2: shift every cell right by one.

**Why counts stay correct.** Setting bit 1 never changes bit 0, and counting reads only bit 0.

lines.text: Visit every cell once in the first pass.
`& 1` keeps only bit 0, the **current** generation, so a neighbour that already has its next state stored in bit 1 still counts correctly.
If the cell lives next generation, set bit 1 (`|= 2`). Bit 0 is untouched, so other cells still read this cell's old state.
Second pass: drop bit 0 and move bit 1 down. Every cell now holds just the new state.

notes.c: The grid is the input itself; only the column-size array is new.

steps.text: Each cell is 0 or 1 now: bit 0 is 'alive this generation'. Bit 1 is free to hold next generation.

First pass: count neighbours with `value & 1` (the old state, even in cells already updated) and set bit 1 (add 2) where the cell lives next. 3 = alive now and next; 2 = born; 1 = dies; 0 = stays empty.

panels.label: old in bit 0, new in bit 1

steps.text: Second pass: shift every cell right by one bit, keeping only the new state.

walk.title: Keep the old state in bit 0 and write the new state into bit 1 of the same cell. Shift right at the end.

takeaways.md:
- **Simultaneous in-place updates:** keep old and new states in different bits of the same cell.
- Always read through a mask that sees only the old state.
- **Pitfall:** writing the new state directly (later cells read updated neighbours).
